title: SNPnexus: an enhanced web platform for large-scale and multi-sample variant analysis (2025 update).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full Europe PMC supplement (0.23 MB) and opened all four Excel tables with pandas: S1 = 24 rows listing pathogenicity-prediction tools and their score cut-offs, S2 = 60 rows of source-database download URLs and versions, S3 = a 22-feature x 8-tool comparison table, S4 = 12 rows of query-runtime benchmarks. Fetched the live site homepage (93 KB HTML); its embedded config shows max 150,000 variants and 6 files per query. Probed /v4/, /v4/downloads/, /v4/guide/ (all HTTP 404 on this host). No bulk download, FTP path or data file link appears anywhere on the homepage (only /about, /example, /guide, /news, /publications).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The data availability statement says only that the website is free and needs no registration; it names no repository, accession or downloadable dataset. A web search confirms a programmatic API is still 'under development' and not released. The internal composition and row counts of SNPnexus's annotation database were never visible to me — the platform returns annotations only in response to a user-submitted variant list.

a1_downloadable.note: There is no dataset to download. SNPnexus is a query-only web front end: you paste in your own variants (max 150,000, verified in the page's embedded config) and it returns annotations. No bulk dump, no FTP, no accession; the REST API is announced as 'coming months'. The only files that actually download are four small supplementary spreadsheets that document the tool, not data.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No outcome column exists anywhere in the downloadable material. The four supplementary tables I opened hold tool metadata (source URLs, score thresholds, feature comparisons, runtimes). Any label — e.g. whether a variant causes disease — would have to be constructed from a separate resource such as ClinVar and then joined in.

a3_inputs_present.note: The inputs are also absent: the user supplies the variants. Supplementary Table S2 is a 60-row list of pointers to other people's files (UCSC, Ensembl, and similar), i.e. references rather than data.

a4_units_stated.note: Where numbers do appear they are labelled: Supplementary Table S1 gives each predictor's score cut-off, S4 gives runtimes in seconds. This is the one Part A item that passes, and it is about documentation tables, not a modelling dataset.

a5_enough_rows.note: Largest downloadable table has 60 rows (Supplementary Table S2, verified by opening the file). The others are 24, 22 and 12 rows. Far below the ~1,500-row threshold.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small — but only because there is nothing substantive to load.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper's claimed 150,000-variant query cap matches the live site's embedded configuration (max_number_variants: 150000). No dataset row counts are claimed, so nothing else to reconcile.

a8_label_provenance.note: Fatal even if the data were downloadable. SNPnexus's core content is in silico pathogenicity predictions — Supplementary Table S1 lists the predictors and their thresholds (SIFT, PolyPhen2 and 22 other rows). Training on those columns means distilling other models' outputs, not learning from any physical measurement.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible: the paper supplies a web annotation service, not a dataset with inputs and an outcome.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use multi-source annotations of a DNA change to predict whether that change causes disease.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would feed a model the annotation profile SNPnexus returns for each DNA variant — location in a gene, population frequency, conservation, regulatory context. Number of examples: unknown, because the underlying database cannot be downloaded in bulk.
plain_idea.predict: Whether the variant is disease-causing. The true answer would have to come from clinical-genetics curation in ClinVar, a separate public database of clinically interpreted variants; SNPnexus itself supplies no verdicts of its own.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Clinical genetics labs must decide which of thousands of variants in a patient's genome to report, so better ranking saves expert review time. But this paper contributes nothing new to that — it repackages annotations anyone can already download from the original sources it lists.

ml_idea: None viable from this paper. The only plausible task — predicting variant pathogenicity from aggregated annotations — needs data this paper does not provide, and its headline annotation columns are other predictors' outputs, so a model trained on them would learn those predictors rather than biology. The genuinely useful parts (ClinVar labels, gnomAD frequencies, conservation scores) are all better obtained directly from the primary resources that Supplementary Table S2 simply links to.

effort.compute_note: Only the 0.23 MB supplement was loaded, in under a second with pandas. No modelling workload exists to estimate.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Look for a bulk download link on snpnexus.org — there is none, and the API is unreleased. Two minutes, and it ends the evaluation.

verdict_reason: This is a web-server update paper, not a dataset. Part A fails four ways, each independently fatal. A1: nothing downloads — the platform annotates variants you submit, there is no database dump, no FTP and no released API (the paper's data availability statement points only at the homepage). A5: the four supplementary spreadsheets I opened contain 60, 24, 22 and 12 rows of tool documentation and runtime benchmarks. A2: no outcome column exists in any of them. A8 is the deepest problem — SNPnexus's main content is other tools' in silico pathogenicity scores (Supplementary Table S1 lists them with their thresholds), so any model trained on it would be copying those predictors instead of learning from measurements. Anyone wanting these annotations should take them from the primary sources Supplementary Table S2 links to.
